descriptive_title: Grade 1 Mathematics: Demonstrations — Canadian Coins and Bills (F1.1)
subject: Mathematics

curriculum_expectations.F1.1: identify the various Canadian coins up to 50¢ and coins and bills up to $50, and compare their values

unit_overview: A 5-day Grade 1 unit on Canadian money (F1.1) framed around 'Our Classroom Market' — Penny the Penguin Shopkeeper and Coin Cassie the Cashier. Day 1 introduces COINS UP TO 50¢ (penny historical, nickel, dime, quarter, 50¢). Day 2 adds the LOONIE ($1) and TOONIE ($2). Day 3 introduces BILLS up to $20. Day 4 introduces $50 bill and compares values. Day 5 closes with a Big Market Capstone where children buy and sell. Each lesson includes an expanded_walkthrough.
unit_learning_goal: Children will identify Canadian coins up to 50¢ and coins/bills up to $50 and compare their values.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Canadian coins up to 50¢: nickel, dime, quarter, 50¢. They have DIFFERENT VALUES.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can name coins up to 50¢ and their values.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Penny shows 4 coins; children sort and name them.

lesson_arc.big_idea: The LOONIE = $1. The TOONIE = $2. They are CANADIAN coins.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can identify the loonie and toonie.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Penny adds loonie + toonie; children sort 6 coins.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Canadian BILLS: $5, $10, $20. Each has a different COLOUR and PERSON.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can identify bills up to $20.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Cassie shows bills; children identify by colour.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We COMPARE money values: more, less, equal. $50 is MORE than $20.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Penny and Cassie compare; children rank 6 amounts.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Shoppers IDENTIFY money and COMPARE values to buy and sell.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can identify and compare Canadian money.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Children rotate 4 stations: coins, bills, compare, buy.

pedagogical_notes: Grade 1 introduces Canadian coins up to 50¢ and bills up to $50.
Skip the ¢ vs $ symbol confusion until Grade 2.
Use REAL Canadian context: loonie and toonie are unique to Canada.
Compare values with words first (more/less/equal), numbers second.
End with a market simulation — buying makes money real.
canadian_context_notes: Loonie ($1) features a loon — Canadian symbol.
Toonie ($2) features a polar bear — Canadian Arctic.
Nickel features a beaver — Canadian symbol.
Quarter has a caribou — Canadian wildlife.
